lessonTitle: Neural Tube Defects, Pharyngeal Arches and Clefts

blocks.text: A routine mid-pregnancy ultrasound shows a fluid-filled sac on the lower back of a fetus, and the mother's blood test earlier showed a raised alpha-fetoprotein. Weeks before she knew she was pregnant, a sheet of tissue folded into a tube and failed to close at one end. The same early weeks also shape the face and neck from a set of arches.

blocks.markdown: In the third and fourth weeks the **neural plate** folds to form the neural tube. The tube zips closed from the middle towards both ends, leaving openings called **neuropores**. The cranial neuropore closes at about day 25 and the caudal neuropore at about day 27 to 28. Failure of closure produces a **neural tube defect (NTD)**. Because closure occurs so early, defects arise before many women realise they are pregnant.

blocks.title: Neural tube defect
blocks.text: A congenital malformation due to incomplete closure of the neural tube or the structures that cover it. It ranges from a hidden vertebral arch defect to complete absence of the brain.

rows: Spina bifida occulta
Vertebral arch fails to fuse; no herniation
Often asymptomatic; may show a tuft of hair or dimple over the lumbar spine
Meningocele
Herniation of meninges through a vertebral defect
Sac of CSF covered by skin or membrane; cord usually normal
Myelomeningocele
Herniation of meninges and neural tissue
Sac containing spinal cord or roots; leg weakness and bladder problems
Anencephaly
Failure of the cranial neuropore to close
Absence of most of the brain and skull vault; incompatible with life
blocks.caption: Spectrum of neural tube defects from mild to severe.

blocks.markdown: **Folic acid.** Folate is needed for cell division and DNA synthesis in the rapidly growing neural tube. Adequate folic acid before conception and in early pregnancy substantially reduces the risk of NTDs. Women at higher risk, for example with a previous affected pregnancy, diabetes or on certain anticonvulsants, receive individual advice from clinicians. Open NTDs release alpha-fetoprotein into amniotic fluid and maternal blood, so raised levels prompt ultrasound examination.

blocks.title: Classifying a lumbar swelling
blocks.prompt: A newborn has a skin-covered sac over the lumbar spine containing nerve roots, with weak legs. The vertebral arches below are open. Classify the lesion and explain the weakness.

steps.text: A sac through a vertebral defect indicates a spina bifida cystica defect.
Neural tissue in the sac makes it a myelomeningocele (a meningocele contains only meninges and CSF).
Roots of the cauda equina or spinal cord in the sac are damaged or tethered, producing lower-limb weakness and often bladder and bowel problems.
The root cause is incomplete closure of the caudal neuropore region.

blocks.answer: Myelomeningocele, with weakness due to involvement of neural tissue.

blocks.markdown: **Pharyngeal arches.** The pharyngeal (branchial) arches are paired structures in the neck of the embryo. Each has a core of mesoderm and neural crest, a cranial nerve, an arch artery and a cartilage. They are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 in humans (the fifth does not form as a separate structure). The pouches between them on the inside of the pharynx also form definite structures.

rows: 1 (mandibular)
Trigeminal (V), mainly maxillary and mandibular divisions
Malleus, incus, mandible (from Meckel's cartilage area)
Muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini
2 (hyoid)
Facial (VII)
Stapes, styloid process, lesser horn and upper body of hyoid
Muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric
Glossopharyngeal (IX)
Greater horn and lower body of hyoid
Stylopharyngeus
4 and 6
Vagus (X): superior laryngeal (4) and recurrent laryngeal (6)
Laryngeal cartilages
Pharyngeal constrictors, cricothyroid (4), other intrinsic laryngeal muscles (6)
blocks.caption: Major derivatives of the pharyngeal arches.

blocks.title: Deducing the arch from a deficit
blocks.prompt: A child has conductive hearing loss from absence of the stapes and also weakness of facial expression on one side. Which arch is implicated and why?

steps.text: The stapes is a derivative of the second arch.
Muscles of facial expression are second-arch muscles supplied by the facial nerve.
Both findings share one embryological origin, so a single second-arch defect explains them.

blocks.markdown: **Cleft lip and palate.** The face forms from the frontonasal prominence, the paired maxillary prominences and the paired mandibular prominences. The upper lip forms when each maxillary prominence fuses with the medial nasal prominence (the intermaxillary segment) at about weeks 5 to 6. Failure of this fusion leaves a **cleft lip**, usually lateral to the midline. The palate forms in two parts: the primary palate from the intermaxillary segment and the secondary palate from palatal shelves that grow from the maxillary prominences. Around weeks 7 to 8 the shelves move from a vertical to a horizontal position and fuse with each other, with the nasal septum and with the primary palate at about week 10 to 12. Failure of fusion causes **cleft palate**.

items: Maxillary prominence fuses with the medial nasal prominence to form the upper lip.
Palatal shelves elevate from vertical to horizontal.
Shelves fuse with each other in the midline and with the nasal septum.
Shelves fuse anteriorly with the primary palate.

blocks.title: Failure of fusion explains clefts
blocks.text: Clefts are not missing tissue but tissue that did not meet. The site of the cleft tells you which prominences or palatal shelves failed to fuse.

blocks.title: Prevention is before conception
blocks.text: Because the neural tube closes at about four weeks, folic acid and risk review must begin before conception. Waiting for a positive pregnancy test may be too late.

points: Neural tube closes at about days 25 and 27 to 28; failure causes anencephaly, meningocele, myelomeningocele or spina bifida occulta, and folic acid before conception reduces risk.

Arch 1 gives malleus, incus and mastication muscles via V; arch 2 gives stapes, hyoid parts and facial expression via VII; arch 3 gives stylopharyngeus via IX; arches 4 and 6 give laryngeal structures via X.
Cleft lip is failed fusion of maxillary and medial nasal prominences; cleft palate is failed fusion of palatal shelves.

questions.stem: A newborn has a lumbar sac containing meninges and CSF only; the spinal cord is normal and the legs move normally. Which diagnosis fits best?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: meninges and CSF without neural tissue form a meningocele.
distractorRationale.b: Myelomeningocele includes neural tissue and causes deficits.
distractorRationale.c: Anencephaly involves the brain and skull.
distractorRationale.d: Spina bifida occulta has no sac.

questions.explanation: A meningocele contains meninges and CSF but not neural tissue, so neurological function is usually preserved. Neural tissue in the sac would make it a myelomeningocele.

questions.stem: Which neuropore failure leads to anencephaly?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: failure of the cranial neuropore to close causes anencephaly.
distractorRationale.b: Caudal neuropore failure leads to defects of the lower spine.
distractorRationale.c: The optic stalk is part of eye development.
distractorRationale.d: Neural crest migration relates to other anomalies.

questions.explanation: The cranial neuropore closes at about day 25, and failure leaves the developing brain exposed and degenerating. Caudal failure produces spinal defects.

questions.stem: A woman planning a pregnancy asks why folate matters. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Adequate folic acid before conception and in early pregnancy reduces the risk of neural tube defects
Folic acid prevents cleft palate in all cases
Folic acid closes the neural tube after birth
It has no effect before pregnancy is confirmed

questions.correctOptionText: Adequate folic acid before conception and in early pregnancy reduces the risk of neural tube defects

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it reduces NTD risk, and benefit depends on taking it before the tube closes.
distractorRationale.b: It does not prevent all clefts.
distractorRationale.c: The neural tube closes in the embryo, not after birth.
distractorRationale.d: Waiting until confirmed pregnancy misses the closure period.

questions.explanation: The neural tube closes by about week 4, so folate must be adequate before then. Preconception supplementation is why women planning pregnancy are advised to start early.

questions.stem: A mother has a raised amniotic alpha-fetoprotein level. Which condition is the most likely cause?

options.text: Cleft lip with normal neural tube

distractorRationale.a: Correct: open NTDs leak alpha-fetoprotein into the amniotic fluid.
distractorRationale.b: Pyloric stenosis is not detected by AFP.
distractorRationale.d: Cleft lip is not typically associated with raised AFP.

questions.explanation: Alpha-fetoprotein from the fetal circulation leaks into amniotic fluid and maternal blood when the neural tube is open. A raised level therefore prompts imaging for NTD.

questions.stem: Which structures are derived from the first pharyngeal arch?

options.text: Muscles of mastication and the malleus
Muscles of facial expression and stapes
Stylopharyngeus and the greater horn of the hyoid
Intrinsic laryngeal muscles and thyroid cartilage

questions.correctOptionText: Muscles of mastication and the malleus

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the first arch gives mastication muscles and the malleus (V).
distractorRationale.b: These belong to the second arch.
distractorRationale.c: These belong to the third arch.
distractorRationale.d: These belong to the fourth and sixth arches.

questions.explanation: The first arch is supplied by the trigeminal nerve and gives rise to muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric and the malleus and incus.

questions.stem: A child with a recurrent laryngeal nerve defect has weakness of most intrinsic laryngeal muscles. Which arch is primarily involved?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the recurrent laryngeal nerve belongs to the sixth arch.
distractorRationale.d: Third arch supplies stylopharyngeus via IX.

questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is the nerve of the sixth arch and supplies most intrinsic laryngeal muscles. The superior laryngeal nerve belongs to the fourth arch.

questions.stem: Cleft lip results from failure of fusion between the maxillary prominence and the medial nasal prominence.
questions.explanation: The upper lip forms when each maxillary prominence meets the medial nasal prominence. If this fusion fails, a cleft appears lateral to the midline.

questions.stem: In cleft palate, which event has failed?

options.text: Fusion of the palatal shelves with each other and the nasal septum
Formation of the second arch cartilage

questions.correctOptionText: Fusion of the palatal shelves with each other and the nasal septum

distractorRationale.a: Correct: palatal shelves must fuse in the midline.
distractorRationale.c: The second arch relates to stapes and facial muscles.
distractorRationale.d: Midgut rotation relates to the gut.

questions.explanation: The secondary palate forms from palatal shelves that must elevate and fuse. Failure of this fusion leaves an open cleft between mouth and nose.

questions.stem: Describe the embryological basis of a cleft lip and a cleft palate, and explain why they may occur separately.
markingGuide: Lip forms from fusion of the maxillary prominence with the medial nasal prominence.
Cleft lip results from failure of this fusion.
Palate forms from the primary palate and palatal shelves.
Shelves elevate and fuse in the midline; failure gives cleft palate.
Different structures fuse at different times, so one can fail alone.
questions.explanation: Lip and palate are formed by different fusion events at different times. Failure of one does not necessarily imply failure of the other.

questions.stem: List the nerve and two derivatives (one skeletal, one muscular) for each of the first and second pharyngeal arches.
markingGuide: Arch 1 derivatives: malleus or incus; muscles of mastication or mylohyoid.
Arch 2 derivatives: stapes or styloid process; muscles of facial expression or stapedius.
Correct pairing of nerve and arch.
questions.explanation: Each arch carries its own nerve, and the muscles of the arch are innervated by that nerve. Knowing the nerve lets you identify the arch from a muscle.
